linen.origin: Linen is made from the bast fiber of fiber flax, Linum usitatissimum. The fiber lies in bundles in the outer stem, between the bark and the woody core that becomes the waste material called shive, and technical fiber strands can run almost the full length of the stem. For that reason fiber flax is pulled from the ground rather than cut, preserving length for long-line yarn. Fiber flax is grown in cool, moist temperate climates, and northwestern Europe has a long-established growing and scutching industry.
linen.structure: Flax fiber is hierarchical. The individual plant cells, called elementary or ultimate fibers, are polygonal in cross-section, roughly pentagonal to octagonal, and average about 15 to 18 micrometers in diameter. Each has a thin primary wall, a thick cellulose-rich secondary wall dominated by the S2 layer, and a narrow central lumen. Elementary fibers overlap along their length and are cemented by pectin and hemicellulose into technical fiber bundles. Transverse dislocations visible under polarized light, called nodes or kink bands, are local compressive defects along the fiber; they help identification and can act as starting points for tensile failure. Cellulose microfibrils lie close to the fiber axis, which contributes to high stiffness and low extension.
linen.process: After pulling, the stems are retted so that microbial enzymes break down the pectins binding fiber to stem. Dew or field retting, the most common method today, leaves the flax in swaths for about three to six weeks, where rain, dew and soil microorganisms act on it; it usually gives grayer fiber. Water retting and enzyme retting give whiter fiber, and over-retting degrades the cellulose. Dried straw is broken and scutched to knock out shive, then hackled (combed) to split and parallelize the long line fiber and separate the short tow. Fine line yarns are traditionally wet spun through hot water, which softens the residual gums so the bundles can be drafted finely; tow is usually dry spun.
linen.performance: Because its cellulose is highly ordered and oriented, flax is strong and stiff with little stretch. That gives linen its crisp hand but also poor wrinkle recovery, and repeated sharp folding along the same line can break fibers at the crease, especially at weak points such as kink bands. Linen absorbs moisture readily and releases it quickly, which contributes to its cool feel, and it tolerates high ironing temperatures. It takes the same dye classes as cotton, such as reactive and vat dyes, though its compact structure can make penetration less even. Like other cellulosic fibers it chars rather than melts and is vulnerable to mildew in damp storage.
linen.identify: Burn tests are indicative only and need fire precautions; linen burns like cotton, with a paper-like smell and soft gray ash. The microscope is more informative: flax shows straight, bamboo-like fibers with cross markings at nodes and kink bands, a polygonal cross-section and a narrow lumen, and no ribbon convolutions like cotton. Separating flax from hemp is harder and may require several methods together, such as a drying-twist test, lignin staining and spectroscopy. Slub-yarn cotton, viscose and polyester fabrics are often sold as having a linen look.
linen.labeling: In the United States, linen is disclosed by its fiber name and percentage by weight under the Textile Fiber Products Identification Act (15 U.S.C. 70 et seq.) and 16 CFR Part 303; linen-look fabrics must be named by their actual fibers. In the EU, Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011 governs textile fiber names. Private origin marks exist for European-grown flax and linen, and they differ in whether they cover only cultivation and scutching or also spinning, weaving and finishing, so the certificate scope matters. Organic flax can be certified through standards such as GOTS or OCS.
linen.past: Flax has been cultivated for fiber since antiquity, and for most of its history the labor of pulling, retting, breaking, scutching, hackling and spinning was done by hand, largely within households and local workshops. Retting practice shaped both fiber color and landscape: water retting in ponds and rivers produced pale fiber but polluted water, while dew retting on the field became the dominant method in modern production. Mechanized hackling and wet spinning allowed fine line yarns to be produced industrially in the nineteenth century. Current research treats the flax bundle as a natural composite, studying kink bands and elementary fiber properties for use in fiber-reinforced plastics.
